original_value: Global Local Climate Zone (LCZ) maps, indicating urban structures and land use, are crucial for Urban Heat Island (UHI) studies and also as starting points to better understand the spatio-temporal dynamics of cities worldwide. However, reliable LCZ maps are not available on a global scale, hindering scientific progress across a range of disciplines that study the functionality of sustainable cities. As a first step towards large-scale LCZ mapping, this paper tries to provide guidance about data/feature choice. To this end, we evaluate the spectral reflectance and spectral indices of the globally available Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 imagery, as well as the Global Urban Footprint (GUF) dataset, the OpenStreetMap layers buildings and land use and the Visible Infrared Imager Radiometer Suite (VIIRS)-based Nighttime Light (NTL) data, regarding their relevance for discriminating different Local Climate Zones (LCZs). Using a Residual convolutional neural Network (ResNet), a systematic analysis of feature importance is performed with a manually-labeled dataset containing nine cities located in Europe. Based on the investigation of the data and feature choice, we propose a framework to fully exploit the available datasets. The results show that GUF, OSM and NTL can contribute to the classification accuracy of some LCZs with relatively few samples, and it is suggested that Landsat-8 and Sentinel-2 spectral reflectances should be jointly used, for example in a majority voting manner, as proven by the improvement from the proposed framework, for large-scale LCZ mapping.

result.paraphrase: Global Local Climate Zone (LCZ) maps, which depict urban form and land use, are important for Urban Heat Island (UHI) research and for improving understanding of the spatio-temporal dynamics of cities worldwide. Yet reliable LCZ maps are not available globally, which slows scientific progress across many disciplines concerned with sustainable-city functionality. As an initial step toward large-scale LCZ mapping, this paper offers guidance on data and feature selection. We assess the spectral reflectance and spectral indices from globally available Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 imagery, along with the Global Urban Footprint (GUF) dataset, OpenStreetMap building and land-use layers, and Visible Infrared Imager Radiometer Suite (VIIRS)-based Nighttime Light (NTL) data, for their ability to distinguish different Local Climate Zones (LCZs). A systematic feature-importance analysis is conducted with a Residual convolutional neural Network (ResNet) using a manually labeled dataset of nine European cities. On the basis of this examination of data and feature choice, we propose a framework that fully exploits the available datasets. The results indicate that GUF, OSM, and NTL can improve classification accuracy for some LCZs with relatively small sample sizes, and they suggest that Landsat-8 and Sentinel-2 spectral reflectances should be combined, for instance through majority voting, as shown by the performance gains from the proposed framework for large-scale LCZ mapping.
